title: Whole report vs partial report

a.definition: The person sees a flashed array of letters and then names as many as they can. In Sperling's (1960) display that was 12 letters in three rows of four.

b.definition: A tone played after the display disappears tells the person which one row to name. They cannot know in advance which row will be cued, so they cannot memorize just one.

diff: Whole report averaged about 4.5 of 12 letters (about 37.5 percent), but partial report averaged about 3.3 of 4 letters (about 82 percent) whichever row was cued. Because people could report almost any row they were cued to, information about all the rows had to be available at the start. The whole-report limit is therefore a limit on how much can be reported before the trace fades, not on how much was perceived.
example: Sperling (1960) flashed three rows of four letters (X M L T, A F N B, C D Z P). People reported only a few when asked for everything, but nearly all of whichever row the tone picked out.
watch: The 82 percent is accuracy on the cued row. It does not mean people stored every letter perfectly. The tone only came after the display was gone, which is what shows all rows were available at first.

title: Immediate vs delayed partial report

a.definition: The cue tone comes right as the display ends, so the person selects the cued row while the trace is still strong. Accuracy was about 3.3 of 4 letters (about 82 percent).

b.definition: The cue tone is held back by an extra delay before the person selects a row. Accuracy fell to about 1 of 4 letters (25 percent).

diff: The only thing that changes between the two is how long the person waits for the cue, so the drop shows the sensory trace is fading fast. As the cue is delayed, partial-report accuracy falls toward the whole-report level. Sensory memory therefore has a large capacity but a very short duration, with most information lost within about one second unless it is selected.
example: In Sperling (1960), the same cue that gave about 82 percent correct when immediate gave about 25 percent when it arrived after the delay.
watch: The fall does not mean the letters were never seen. It means the representation faded before the cue could be used to select from it.

title: Sensory memory vs short-term memory

a.definition: Briefly retains incoming stimulation for seconds or fractions of a second. It has a very large capacity but fades quickly unless attention selects part of it.

b.definition: Holds about five to seven items for roughly fifteen to twenty seconds. Rehearsal can keep the contents available and move them toward long-term memory.

diff: The two stores of Atkinson and Shiffrin's (1968) modal model differ in how much they hold and how long it lasts. Sensory memory holds a lot for an instant, which is why Sperling's (1960) immediate cue let people report almost any row, and a delayed cue arrived after most of it had faded. Short-term memory holds a little for longer, and attention is what moves selected information from the first into the second.
example: Looking at a phone directory floods sensory memory with many items at once. Attention picks out the one number you want, which puts it in short-term memory, and repeating it keeps it there long enough to dial.
watch: Do not describe short-term memory as just a longer sensory memory. Sensory memory is large and fleeting, while short-term memory is small and depends on selection and rehearsal.

title: Icon vs echo

a.definition: The fleeting visual trace left by stimulation. It is the visual form of sensory memory, and persistence of vision (a sparkler seeming to leave a trail) shows it.

b.definition: The brief continuation of auditory information after a sound ends. It is the auditory form of sensory memory.

diff: Both are sensory memory and both fade within seconds or fractions of a second, so the only difference is the sense involved: seeing for the icon and hearing for the echo. Neither is the durable representation used to remember something much later.
example: Sperling (1960) studied iconic memory with flashed letters. As an illustration of an echo, you can still replay the last few words someone said for a moment after they stop.
watch: A large capacity does not mean a long duration. Both traces decay quickly.

title: Decay vs interference

a.definition: A memory trace weakens simply because time passes. It predicts the same loss at the same delay on every trial.

b.definition: Other memories compete with the one being tested. It predicts that loss depends on how much competing material there is, not only on time.

diff: In Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), participants saw three letters and a number and counted backward by threes for 3 to 18 seconds, which blocks rehearsal. The average over all trials fell steadily, and Peterson and Peterson read that as decay. But at 18 seconds recall was relatively high on trial 1, lower by trial 3, and very low after many trials, so the same delay did far more damage when more earlier sets had piled up. As presented, that trial-by-trial pattern points to proactive interference, which Keppel and Underwood (1962) offered as the alternative account.
example: The same 18-second delay gave high recall on the first trial and very low recall after many trials.
watch: If an answer says forgetting happened 'because of time' but ignores the trial history, it is describing decay when the pattern shows interference.

title: Retroactive vs proactive interference

a.definition: New information disrupts memory for older information. The memory that suffers is the old one, and the competitor arrived later.

b.definition: Old information disrupts memory for newer information. The memory that suffers is the new one, and the competitor arrived earlier.

diff: To label it correctly, first decide which information the person is trying to recall, then ask whether the competing information came before or after it. Earlier competing material is proactive and later competing material is retroactive. Routine events are especially vulnerable because similar memories compete, and both kinds are reduced when events are distinctive.
example: Learning a new phone number and then struggling to recall the old one is retroactive. Previous parking spots making today's spot hard to remember is proactive, and so are earlier trigrams harming recall of the current one in Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959).
watch: Do not pick by which memory is 'newer' in general. The question is always about the direction of harm relative to the item being recalled.

title: Average over all trials vs trial-by-trial recall

a.definition: Pools every trial together, so recall appears to drop steadily as the delay grows from 3 to 18 seconds, as though short-term memory simply decays.

b.definition: Looks at early and late trials separately. Early trials keep high recall even at 18 seconds, and later trials show very low recall at the same delay.

diff: The steep drop in the average comes mostly from the later trials, where proactive interference has built up. Averaging hides the interference behind something that looks like decay. This is why the Brown-Peterson pattern is evidence for interference and not only for time-based decay.
example: In Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), recall at 18 seconds was relatively high on trial one, lower by trial three, and substantially reduced after many trials.
watch: The average blends early trials with high recall and late trials with very low recall, so it hides where the steep drop actually comes from.

title: Maintenance rehearsal vs elaborative rehearsal

a.definition: Repeating information, such as silently saying a label or number, to prolong how long it stays available in short-term memory.

b.definition: Linking new information to knowledge already in long-term memory, such as explaining how it relates to what you know.

diff: Maintenance keeps information alive only while the repeating continues. Elaborative rehearsal adds meaning, which supports learning that lasts longer. Recoding is a third control process: it reorganizes or modifies information that is already in short-term memory.
example: Repeating a label over and over keeps it available (maintenance). Explaining how the label relates to something you already know supports longer-term learning (elaborative).
watch: Repetition is not the same as understanding. If the question stresses meaning or links to existing knowledge, the answer is elaborative.

title: Miller's seven plus or minus two vs three to four items

a.term: Seven plus or minus two units
a.definition: Miller's (1956) estimate of short-term capacity, where a unit can be a digit, word, number or phrase and differs across tasks.

b.definition: Alvarez and Cavanagh's (2004) estimate for visual short-term memory from change detection, where accuracy falls sharply above roughly four items.

diff: Miller's units can hold different amounts of information, so the title does not prove that every system holds exactly seven raw items. The figures come from different places: five to seven is the modal-model estimate for short-term memory, seven plus or minus two is Miller's, and three to four is Alvarez and Cavanagh's (2004) estimate for visual objects, where colored squares gave a higher estimated capacity than complex polygons or shaded cubes. Different tasks need not measure one identical capacity.
example: In Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004), the first array stayed up for 100 milliseconds, the second for 2,000 milliseconds, and people judged whether the two matched.
watch: Do not treat seven as a universal limit for visual memory. The amount of information in each object matters.

title: Single item vs chunk

a.definition: One basic unit, such as a single digit, letter or word.

b.definition: A larger meaningful unit built from smaller ones, such as a familiar group of digits.

diff: Chunking raises effective capacity by letting each slot in short-term memory carry more information, so the same limited number of units holds more. The gain comes from knowledge-based organization, not from enlarging every raw limit equally.
example: Ericsson and colleagues (1980) trained a student to reach a digit span of 79 by treating strings of digits as familiar running times, so each running time was one chunk.
watch: A big span after training does not mean the memory system itself got bigger. It means each unit holds more.

title: Episodic vs semantic memory

a.definition: Memory for personal events tied to a particular time and place. Tulving described it as a kind of mental time travel.

b.definition: Memory for facts and general knowledge that is not tied to the moment you learned it.

diff: Both are branches of declarative memory inside long-term memory, and the other major branch of long-term memory is procedural memory, which concerns skills. Episodic memory answers 'what happened to me then', and semantic memory answers 'what do I know'. They are classified by function, not by how long they last.
example: As an illustration, remembering one particular birthday party is episodic, and knowing what a birthday is is semantic.
watch: Neither is an extra short-term store. They sit in long-term memory.

title: Duration vs capacity

a.definition: How long information stays available in short-term memory, roughly fifteen to twenty seconds without rehearsal.

b.definition: How much information can be held at once, traditionally about seven plus or minus two units.

diff: Duration is how long information stays available, and capacity is how much can be held at once. Each can be changed by a strategy: rehearsal prolongs duration, and chunking raises effective capacity. So when a result changes, ask which strategy was used and not only which memory system is involved.
example: Counting backward blocks rehearsal in Brown (1958) and Peterson and Peterson (1959), so a trigram is lost within about fifteen to twenty seconds. Ericsson and colleagues (1980) raised a digit span to 79 by chunking.
watch: A question about 'how long' is duration and 'how much' is capacity. Mixing them up is a common slip.

title: Short-term memory vs working memory

a.definition: A single component that holds what has been selected for a short time. Rehearsal keeps its contents available, and the emphasis is on temporary availability.

b.definition: A limited-capacity system for the temporary storage and manipulation of information, with a central executive, a phonological loop and a visuospatial sketchpad.

diff: The working-memory model treats memory as active: information is held and worked on at the same time. It also separates verbal and auditory information from visual and spatial information, with the central executive coordinating them. Baddeley added the episodic buffer in 2000, so it belongs to the expanded model.
example: In 43 × 6, the 8 from 3 × 6 = 18 is held (storage) while the 1 is carried and 6 × 4 = 24 is computed (an operation). The 8 has to survive while other steps run.
watch: Do not describe working memory as passive storage. Comprehension, learning and reasoning need holding and operating together.

title: Phonological loop vs visuospatial sketchpad

a.definition: Maintains verbal and auditory information, with a phonological store that holds it and an articulatory rehearsal process that repeats the sounds, even silently.

b.definition: Holds visual information (what something looks like) and spatial information (where its parts are and how they are arranged).

diff: Ask whether the content is sounds and words or shapes and locations. Brooks's (1968) opposite results show the two are at least partly independent. Both interact with long-term knowledge, so one calculation can use verbal rehearsal of a result together with a picture of the digits.
example: A remembered sentence uses the loop. The remembered shape of an F uses the sketchpad.
watch: The central executive is not a store for any particular kind of content. It directs and coordinates the other two.

title: Brooks's sentence task vs F task

a.definition: People memorized a sentence and decided for each word whether it was a noun, responding by speaking or by pointing. Pointing was easier.

b.definition: People memorized the shape of an F and classified each corner as inside or outside, responding by speaking or by pointing. Speaking was easier.

diff: In the sentence task, holding the sentence used the phonological loop, so speaking the answers competed with it. In the F task, following the F used the sketchpad, so pointing to spatially arranged responses competed with it. A task is easier when the information held and the operation performed use different types of short-term memory.
example: Holding a sentence while speaking answers interfered in the sentence task, and holding an F while pointing to answers interfered in the F task.
watch: Memorize the logic, not just the result: the easier response is the one that uses the other system.

title: Phonological store vs articulatory rehearsal

a.definition: The part of the phonological loop that holds verbal and auditory information for a short time.

b.definition: The part that keeps the contents active by repeating the sounds, even silently.

diff: Articulatory suppression, speaking while trying to memorize, occupies the rehearsal process. That reduces recall, and it reduces both the word-length effect (because short words no longer win by being quicker to rehearse) and the phonological similarity effect (because converting seen items into sounds is disrupted).
example: As an illustration, repeating an unrelated word while trying to memorize a list leaves the rehearsal process busy.
watch: Suppression does not erase the store. It blocks the process that refreshes it.

title: Word-length effect vs phonological similarity effect

a.definition: Lists of short words are remembered better than lists of long words, because longer words take more time to say and rehearse.

b.definition: Items that sound alike are confused with each other, even when they look different.

diff: Word length is about the time needed to rehearse the items, and similarity is about overlapping sound codes. Both support the idea that verbal maintenance depends on sound-based codes and speech-related rehearsal, and articulatory suppression reduces both.
example: Word length: Baddeley and colleagues (1975, 1984) found more short words were recalled than long words, and Ellis and Hennelly (1980) found Welsh-English bilingual children had a shorter digit span in Welsh because Welsh number names take longer to say. Phonological similarity: E is confused with B because they sound alike.
watch: Span tracks how much can be said in about 1.5 to 2 seconds, so the language difference follows the time to say the number names and not the numbers themselves.

title: Central executive vs the two storage systems

a.definition: Directs and maintains attention, divides attention, switches it when the task changes, suppresses irrelevant information, coordinates the other components and performs calculations.

b.definition: Hold and rehearse particular kinds of content: verbal and auditory for the loop, visual and spatial for the sketchpad.

diff: The executive is about control, and the other two are about content. Naming a controller does not explain how control is done, which is why the executive is criticized as a homunculus, and it is today often split into updating, shifting and inhibition (Miyake and colleagues, 2000).
example: As an illustration, following a phone number while giving directions needs the executive to split attention while the loop rehearses the digits.
watch: Do not describe the executive as storing information.

title: Updating vs shifting

a.definition: Changing the information currently being maintained as new information arrives.

b.definition: Changing the task or operation being performed.

diff: Miyake and colleagues (2000) separate these two from inhibition, which suppresses information or responses that interfere with the goal. Updating is about the contents of memory, shifting is about the operation, and inhibition is about what to block.
example: As an illustration, replacing the contents you are holding with new ones is updating, switching from adding to multiplying is shifting, and ignoring a distracting number is inhibition.
watch: All three are functions inside what would otherwise be one broad label, the executive.

title: Original three-part model vs the episodic buffer

a.definition: The central executive, phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad proposed by Baddeley and Hitch (1974).

b.definition: A fourth component of limited capacity, about four chunks, that binds information from the loop, the sketchpad and long-term memory into integrated episodes.

diff: The buffer is needed because people can immediately recall about 16 words from a meaningful sentence, more than their span for unrelated words, since meaning and long-term language knowledge let the words stay connected. Some amnesic patients can immediately recall a just-heard story, which suggests immediate retention of an organized episode can survive when longer-term memory is impaired.
example: A sentence's words are kept together as connected material, not as 16 separate items.
watch: The buffer is not part of the original three-component proposal.

title: High-capacity vs low-capacity participants

a.definition: Kept irrelevant blue bars out of working memory, so adding two blue distractors to two red targets changed their response little.

b.definition: Let the irrelevant bars in, so the same distractors raised their response toward the four-item level.

diff: Vogel and colleagues (2005) recorded event-related potentials during a task where red bars were shown for 100 milliseconds and held across a 900 millisecond retention interval. Capacity was positively correlated with filtering efficiency, so people with higher capacity are also less distracted, and a lower score can reflect competing material occupying processing the targets needed.
example: Two red targets alone against two red plus two blue: the ERP response barely changed for high-capacity people and rose for low-capacity people.
watch: Capacity here is not only about holding items. It is also about keeping the wrong ones out.

title: Rotating a representation vs storing a fixed picture

a.definition: Holding the image as it was seen, with no operation applied. If this were all that happened, deciding whether two views match would take about the same time whatever the angle between them.

b.definition: Turning an internal representation to line it up with the other view, in the picture plane or in depth. A bigger angle needs more turning, so it takes longer.

diff: Shepard and Metzler (1971) showed pairs of block-built objects at different orientations and asked whether they matched. For picture-plane pairs, reaction time rose approximately linearly with the angle, so small angles were answered faster than large ones. A static copy would predict no angle effect, so the pattern points to an active operation on a spatial representation.
example: People judged whether pairs of block-built objects matched, and small angles were answered faster than large ones.
watch: The evidence is the shape of the reaction-time curve and not what people say they felt, and the linear pattern was for picture-plane pairs.

title: Short-term memory vs long-term memory

a.definition: Holds about five to seven items for roughly fifteen to twenty seconds and is easily disrupted by interruption and interference.

b.definition: Retains large amounts of information for years or even decades.

diff: Rehearsal moves information from short-term toward long-term memory, and retrieval moves it back, so the flow goes both ways and not only toward storage. Short-term memory is the active window on the present, and long-term memory is the large body of knowledge stored outside current awareness.
example: You look up a phone number, repeat it to keep it in short-term memory, and later retrieve it from long-term memory back into short-term memory to dial it.
watch: Do not treat long-term memory as simply more of short-term memory. They differ in capacity and in duration.

title: Declarative vs procedural memory

a.definition: Long-term memory for events and knowledge, with two branches: episodic memory for events and semantic memory for facts.

b.definition: Long-term memory for skills.

diff: The memory tree sorts long-term memory by function and not by how long things last. Declarative memory is what you can state, and procedural memory is what you can do.
example: Knowing what a bicycle is is declarative, and knowing how to ride one is procedural.
watch: Episodic and semantic memory are both inside declarative memory.

title: Encoding, storage and retrieval failure

a.definition: Encoding converts information into a form that can be stored, and storage keeps it.

b.definition: Bringing stored information back out when it is needed.

diff: A failure to remember could come from a problem at any of the three operations, so forgetting on its own does not show which one failed. Memory is also an active system that can organize and even alter information, so it is not a recording kept unchanged.
example: Forgetting a familiar name could mean it was never encoded well, was lost from storage, or cannot be retrieved right now.
watch: Do not name the failed stage from the failure alone.

title: Simple vs complex objects in visual short-term memory

a.definition: Objects such as colored squares need little information to represent, so more of them can be held.

b.definition: Objects such as polygons, shaded cubes or Chinese-character-like forms need more information to represent, so fewer can be held.

diff: Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004) found that same-different performance depends on how complex the stimuli are, so capacity is constrained by the amount of information needed to represent the objects. A capacity for one category of stimulus is not a universal estimate for all visual objects.
example: Colored squares supported a higher estimated capacity than shaded cubes in the change-detection task.
watch: Do not count every object as an equally sized item.
